b.bio: Eusebius Pamphili, born at Caesarea around 260/265, studied under the presbyter Pamphilus and took his name. After Pamphilus's martyrdom (310) he traveled to Tyre and Egypt; by about 313/314 he was bishop of Caesarea. He subscribed to the Creed of Nicaea (325) after first presenting a creed of his own, explaining his subscription in a letter to his diocese, and later wrote against Marcellus of Ancyra. He died 30 May 339. His scholarship centered on the biblical text: he worked with Pamphilus on questions of canon and produced the Onomasticon and gospel canons alongside his historical and apologetic works.
b.s: Called the Father of Church History, he fixed the genres of Christian historiography and apologetic; the library holds his Ecclesiastical History, Chronicle, Preparation for the Gospel, Proof of the Gospel, Life of Constantine, and exegetical commentaries on Psalms and Isaiah.

b.bio: Born at Antwerp in 1649, Schelstrate was a canon of the cathedral there before being summoned to Rome and made assistant librarian of the Vatican Library. The sources credit the summons to Pope Innocent IX, though that pontiff died in 1591, decades before Schelstrate's birth; the name is presumably an error for one of the later Innocents. He became the accredited defender of papal supremacy, attacking Launoy on the Roman primacy, opposing the Gallican declaration of 1682, and disputing with Arnauld, Louis Maimbourg, and Edward Stillingfleet.
b.s: The work held here is his polemic against Maimbourg's conciliarism, arguing that the Council of Constance's decree placing a general council above the pope is textually corrupted, lacked legitimate conciliar authority, and was never approved by Martin V.

b.bio: Étienne Baluze was born at Tulle on 24 November 1630 and died in Paris on 28 July 1718. Educated at the Collège de St Martial in Toulouse, he took minor orders but never went beyond tonsure. He served as secretary to Pierre de Marca, archbishop of Toulouse and later of Paris, whose papers he inherited and edited, including De libertatibus Ecclesiae Gallicanae (1663) and Marca hispanica (1688). From 1667 to 1700 he was librarian to Colbert, assembling a manuscript collection that later enriched the Bibliothèque Nationale. Louis XIV appointed him professor of canon law at the Collège Royal/Collège de France (sources differ on whether this was in 1670 or 1689); in 1710 he was exiled from Paris after publishing material on the House of Auvergne that offended the court.
b.s: The works held here are not treatises of his own theology but the critical apparatus of a pioneering editor: notes, prefaces, chronologies, and collections of formulas attached to his editions of Lactantius, Regino, Burchard, and other patristic and canonical texts.

b.bio: This entry covers a single epistle preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 13, issued in the name of a synod of bishops at Constantinople. The letter confirms the Nicene faith and anathematizes opposing heresies, and holds that the emperor should ratify synodal decrees. It cites Ambrose, which places its composition after his rise as bishop of Milan (374), though no source here fixes the assembly's date or identifies it with either the 381 or the 553 Council of Constantinople.
b.s: A brief conciliar letter showing how eastern synods appealed to imperial authority to enforce doctrinal settlement, preserved among Latin patristic texts alongside Ambrose's correspondence.

b.bio: The library prints the name as E. de Evesham; the work held here, a Life of St. Thomas of Canterbury in PL 190, belongs to Elias of Evesham (Elias Eveshamensis), a Benedictine monk and hagiographer of Evesham Abbey active around 1200. He is credited with a Life of Thomas Becket known in some sources as the Quadrilogus. Other Evesham writers named in the sources — Dominic of Evesham (prior by 1125) and Walter of Evesham (fl. 1320) — are different men and are not this author.
b.s: His Life of Becket is one of the many medieval vitae of the martyred archbishop; the two pages held here defend the writing of saints' lives for God's glory and edification, justify compiling one account from four authors as with the gospels, and report the incorrupt body found at translation, miracles rewarding devotion, and deliverance through invoking the saint.

b.bio: Ebalus of Reims (Ebalus Reminensis) was archbishop of Reims from 1021 until his death on 11 May 1033. Some genealogies identify him as Ebles I, count of Roucy, son of Giselbert of Roucy, though Moranvillé questioned this co-identity, noting that Alberic of Trois-Fontaines spells the name differently ('Roseio' vs 'Roceio') and that Fulbert of Chartres and Hariulf describe the appointment without mentioning a Roucy origin. The library holds one work under his name: a charter of AD 1024 for the monastery of Mouzon.
b.s: His single held work is a monastic charter asserting the restoration of church property to monastic use and the perpetual irrevocability of ecclesiastical grants, naming Adalbero as bishop and Hugh, Harduin and Alulf as archdeacons.

b.bio: Ebbo was born a serf on Charlemagne's royal demesne, was educated at court and given his liberty by Charlemagne, and became librarian and councillor to Louis the Pious, who appointed him Archbishop of Reims in 816. In 822 he went to Rome and obtained from Pope Paschal I a legateship for the North, preaching in Denmark in 823 with Halitgar of Cambrai and Willerich of Bremen. He joined Lothair's rebellion against Louis in 833 and presided at the synod of Soissons that deposed the emperor; after Louis's restoration Ebbo was deposed from Reims, restored briefly under Lothair in 840–841, and died at Hildesheim on 20 March 851.
b.s: The works held here are his apology and confession from his deposition years, defending the canonical restoration of expelled bishops and arguing that yielding to persecutors rather than resisting is lawful, with flight from persecution following Christ's example.

b.bio: Eberhard was abbot of the Benedictine abbey of Tegernsee in Bavaria; Documenta Catholica Omnia dates his Epistolae to 1001–1050. The letters preserved under his name in PL 141 concern the abbey's affairs: disputes over who should hold the office of advocate (Vogt) of the monastery, arguing that an advocate should be appointed by ducal order and monastic counsel and that the duke should appoint Udalric, with named opponents including Poppo, Piligrim and their mother, Penno, and Wolfold; the continued formation of a monk returning to the community; prayer for the dead; unfulfilled vows; and the defense of the church by royal authority after God. The sources say nothing further about his life beyond his abbacy.
b.s: His three pages of letters are a primary witness to how a tenth/eleventh-century abbey fought legal and political battles over its advocacy and property, and to monastic teaching on prayer for the dead.

w: From the Miracles of St. Simeon
On the Abbey of Saint Martin

b.bio: Eberwin was a Benedictine abbot of St. Martin's in Trier, also abbot of Tholey and possibly of St-Paul at Verdun (Germania Sacra notes this only as alleged), attested between roughly 1018 and 1036; Germania Sacra gives a wider range, um 995–1040. In 1026 he made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. He wrote the Vita and Miracles of St. Simeon, the recluse of Trier, and a Vita of Bishop Magnericus of Trier, and perhaps an account of the calamities of his own abbey.
b.s: His works here are hagiographical histories: they present patient endurance under persecution as witnessing holiness, defend recluses enclosed by episcopal authority for prayer, and argue that monasteries must not be alienated as lay benefices, with papal privilege securing monastic election and stability.

b.bio: Ebrardus Watinensis, a canon of the abbey of Watten in the county of Flanders, wrote the Chronicon Watinense around 1080 (the Documenta Catholica Omnia edition dates it 1089). The chronicle traces the origins of the monastery and its region: it identifies the people of Watten with the ancient Batavians, argues that Roman vengeance destroyed that fierce people while providence preserved remnants from extermination, and presents the founding of Watten as fulfilled by divine providence. It disputes accounts favoring Hubert, bishop of Thérouanne, and cites Gregory VII and Orosius. Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand later published it from a manuscript of the abbey of Dunes; it appears in PL 149, columns 1513–1546B.
b.s: His chronicle is an important source for the early history of Flanders and for the abbey of Watten, founded in 1072 by the priest Olfride for canons regular of Saint Augustine.

w: Charter granted to the New Minster of Winchester
Charter in the Council of London
Ecclesiastical Laws of the Council of Brentford
Prayer to Dunstan, Oswald, and Ethelwald

b.bio: Edgar (Eadgar), younger son of King Edmund I and Ælfgifu, was chosen king by the Mercians and Northumbrians in 957 during the revolt against his brother Eadwig, ruling north of the Thames until Eadwig's death on 1 October 959 made him king of all England. His reign was peaceful and free of Viking attack, and he is chiefly remembered as patron of the English Benedictine Reform, working closely with Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, and Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester. He issued legislative codes and standardized the coinage in the early 970s. The DNB gives his birth year as 944; Britannica says 943/944.
b.s: The works held here are royal charters and ecclesiastical law codes — grants to New Minster Winchester and Malmesbury, council decrees from London and Brentford, a prayer invoking Dunstan, Oswald, and Ethelwald, and a charter of Oswadeslau — documents through which Edgar enforced the monastic reform against secular canons and clerics. The library record also shows the collection treating doctrinal themes (providential government, creation ex nihilo, the angelic fall and its punishment), consistent with reform-era ecclesiastical legislation framing monastic life as restoring the angels' fallen office.

b.bio: In the library catalogue, 'The Editors' is a collective editorial heading under the Latin Fathers tradition associated with prefatory texts titled 'To the reader' and 'Admonition', as well as the compilation 'Dogmatic Library of the Fathers II'.
b.s: The heading represents a generic catalogue designation for editorial apparatus and introductory notes rather than a distinct individual historical figure.

b.bio: This entry denotes the editors of the first printed edition of the Ligurinus, catalogued under the Latin Fathers tradition as the contributors of the preface to that edition.
b.s: The editors were responsible for introducing the first printed edition of Gunther of Pairis's medieval epic Ligurinus to early modern readers.

b.bio: None of the surviving records describes this author, and all four Edmunds they cover — Edmund of Abingdon (d. 1240), Edmund Bishop (1846–1917), Edmund Grindal (c. 1519–1583), and Edmund Campion (1540–1581) — are different persons of the same name from other centuries and traditions; their biographies cannot be used for this author. The works held here cite King Edmund twice and treat legal rather than scholastic or polemical topics, suggesting an anonymous compiler of ecclesiastical law circulating under Edmund's name.
b.s: The two texts held here are collections of ecclesiastical laws enforcing clerical chastity according to order, tithes and church dues with excommunication for refusal to pay, penance for homicide before restoration, treatment of sexual sin against vows as homicide, bishops' duty to maintain churches, and exclusion of perjurers and sorcerers from communion without satisfaction.

b.bio: Edward, son of Æthelred II and Emma of Normandy, spent much of his youth in exile at the Norman court during Danish rule over England, and reigned as king of the English until his death on 5 January 1066. Venerated as a saint ('St Edward the Confessor'), he is remembered for his piety. The works held under his name are not theological treatises but documents issued in his name: royal diplomas and codes of law preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 151). The laws attributed to him regulate church dues, tithes, sanctuary, and relations between crown and clergy.
b.s: The works here are diplomas and ecclesiastical laws attributed to Edward's reign, showing how an eleventh-century English king framed royal duty toward the Church—tithes, sanctuary immunity, vicarious satisfaction of vows—and polemicized against withholders of tithes, usurers, and William Rufus.

b.bio:
Edward the Elder (870s?–924) — Edward the Elder was King of the Anglo-Saxons from 899 until his death on 17 July 924, elder son of Alfred the Great and Ealhswith. He defeated a challenge to his succession by his cousin Æthelwold, and with his sister Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, conquered Viking-ruled southern England after a decisive victory over a Northumbrian army in 910. The library holds under his name a short piece of ecclesiastical legislation (PL 138), which cites Alfred, Guthrum, and earlier canons.

Guthrum of the Danes (d. 890) — Guthrum, a Danish leader of the Great Heathen Army, fought Alfred the Great in Wessex and was defeated at Edington in 878. As a condition of surrender he was baptized, taking the name Æthelstan with Alfred as godfather, and thereafter ruled East Anglia as a Christian king until his death around 890. The Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum fixed boundaries between their territories and set wergild values; it is regarded as the foundation of the Danelaw. The work held here under his name is the ecclesiastical-law material associated with that treaty: provisions on baptism, penalties for apostasy and clerical crime, jurisdiction of bishops over clergy, and confession for the condemned.
b.s: The work held here is royal ecclesiastical law: it asserts that secular penalties support amendment of the church, that church peace and royal peace stand equal, that apostasy draws wergild and fine, that clergy answer to bishops in capital cases, and that confession is never denied to the condemned.

w: History of the Translation of Marcellinus and Peter
Rhythm on the passion of Marcellinus and Peter

b.bio: Einhard (also Eginhard), born around 770 in the Maingau, was educated at Fulda and entered Charlemagne's court around 791, where he worked on palace construction at Aachen and Ingelheim. Louis the Pious made him his private secretary in 814; he managed Charlemagne's will and helped facilitate Louis's elevation as co-emperor. He retired from court during the disputes among Louis's sons and died on 14 March 840 at Seligenstadt. Sources give his birth year as c. 770 (Britannica) or c. 775 (Wikipedia); the wider range covers both.
b.s: His Vita Karoli Magni is the principal contemporary biography of Charlemagne, and the works here also include annals of Lorsch, letters, charters, a rhythm on the passion of Marcellinus and Peter, and an account of the translation of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter.

b.bio: Eigil, of noble Norican parents and a relative of Sturm, was sent to Fulda as a boy shortly after Boniface's martyrdom and remained at Sturm's side for twenty years. After the deposition and banishment of Abbot Ratgar, whose severity had divided the monastery, Eigil was elected abbot about 818 and held office until his death in 822; he sought Ratgar's return from Louis the Pious. Candidus Bruun later wrote his biography in prose and verse. Though called a saint, his name appears in no martyrology.
b.s: The works here are his Life of Saint Sturmius, an eyewitness-based account of Fulda's foundation written at Angildruth's request, which defends Sturm's monastic vocation against Lullus and the 'false brothers' and presents the abbey's mission against Saxon paganism.

b.bio: Ellinger was born around 978 in Bavaria to a noble family, educated under Froumund at Tegernsee and at St. Ulrich in Augsburg, with further study at Würzburg and Bamberg (c. 1012–16). He became a monk at Tegernsee before 997 and was installed as abbot there in 1017 by Henry II, on the intervention of Godehard of Niederaltaich. He renewed the school, library, and scriptorium, worked as a copyist and illuminator, and led a Tegernsee reform circle within the Gorze-Trier movement. Monastic resistance forced his resignation in 1026; he was restored in 1031 through Godehard's intervention and charged with rebuilding Benediktbeuern, but Bishop Nitker of Freising deposed him again in 1041. He spent his last years at Niederaltaich, dying at Tegernsee on 13 May 1056.
b.s: The letters held here are polemical defenses of episcopal authority, the rights of benefices against unjust alienation, and the duty of bishops to protect their flocks — written chiefly against Bishop Nitker of Freising and other opponents during the disputes that twice cost him his abbacy.

b.bio: Elpis (also Elphe or Elpide), first wife of the philosopher Boethius, was a Latin poet and hymnographer of the late fifth and early sixth century. She was daughter of Festus, consul at Rome in 472, and sister of the mother of St. Placidus, a disciple of St. Benedict. She died young, at Padua, around 504. Two hymns of praise to the apostles Peter and Paul are traditionally attributed to her; the attribution is uncertain.
b.s: The library holds her hymns (PL 63): verse on prayer to the apostles, who hear prayers and loose sins, on faith now veiled that shall see God face to face, on charity reigning in eternal life, and glory due to the Trinity in unity.

b.bio: Emma of Normandy, daughter of Duke Richard the Fearless and Gunnor, married Æthelred the Unready in 1002 and Cnut the Great in 1017, making her queen of England under both kings and mother of two more: Harthacnut and Edward the Confessor. She was also queen consort of Denmark from 1018 and of Norway from 1028 until Cnut's death on 12 November 1035. In English royal documents she was sometimes known by the name Ælfgifu. After Cnut's death she remained an active political figure at Winchester, where she died on 6 March 1052 and was buried in the Old Minster.
b.s: The work held here is a letter attributed to Emma, preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 141 under the title 'Letter to his children'. Its precise contents and circumstances are not established by the sources consulted.

b.bio: Engelmodus (Angilmod) was a Benedictine monk of Corbie who became bishop of Soissons in 862 and died in 865 (Wikisource alone gives his death as 864). He belongs to the circle of Carolingian poets around Corbie; the work held here is a set of verses addressed to Abbot Radbert — presumably Paschasius Radbertus of Corbie, though no source explicitly makes this identification. He also wrote a Libellus de ordine scrutinii on the examination of candidates.
b.s: The single work here, Verses to Abbot Radbert, is a witness to the literary circle of Corbie in the mid-ninth century rather than a theological argument.

w: Life of St. Mary the Harlot

b.bio: Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373) — Born at Nisibis in Mesopotamia early in the fourth century, Ephrem was baptized by Bishop James of Nisibis, served as a deacon, and after Nisibis was ceded to the Persians in 363 settled at Edessa, where he taught and wrote. He composed hymns, verse homilies, and prose exegesis, and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1920. The library holds two Latin ascetic lives printed under his name in Migne's PL 73.
b.s: The library's two Latin lives under his name narrate sudden conversion from secular life by divine grace, renunciation of possessions, and obedience as excelling all virtues, illustrating how Ephrem's name anchored a large body of later hagiography.

b.bio: Erchambert of Freising, seventh bishop of Freising from 835/836 until his death in 854, came from the Bavarian high nobility of the Huosi and was a nephew of his predecessor Hitto. He was present at the Treaty of Verdun in 843 and by 844 was also abbot of Kempten. He is remembered as an effective promoter of his diocese and was later venerated as a blessed; his remains were moved to Freising cathedral after the secularization.
b.s: The library holds two short pieces under his name: an epistle to his own people and a fragment of historical narrative covering Charles Martel's rise — mayors of the palace holding royal power while kings kept only the name, Chilperic's selection by Merovingian kinship, and Charles's war against Chilperic, Ragenfrid, and Plectrude. The fragment also treats true worship against demonic deception and records Columbanus's prophecy of Chlothar's rule over three kingdoms.

b.bio: Erchempertus, a Benedictine monk of Monte Cassino in the last quarter of the ninth century, wrote the Historia Langobardorum Beneventanorum degentium, a chronicle of the Lombard principality of Benevento. The Cyclopedia adds that he was descended from the dukes of Benevento, was taken prisoner when Pandonulf of Capua took his father's castle in 881, escaped, and became a monk at Monte Cassino; it also credits him with an abbot's office and other works, but these details are not confirmed by the modern sources. His history runs from Duke Arechis II and the Carolingian conquest down to the winter of 888–889, where it stops abruptly. One medieval manuscript survives, from the early fourteenth century.
b.s: His history is a near-contemporary account of the violence among the Lombard princes of southern Italy, read here for its treatment of providence, princely anointing, compelled oaths, and the civil magistrate.

b.bio: Erkembald of Strasbourg (also printed as Erchanbaldus Argentinensis; known in youth as Altrich) was a high-born German cleric ordained priest around 963, made coadjutor to Bishop Udo of Strasbourg, and consecrated bishop on 24 September 965 by Archbishop William of Mainz (Wikidata/Catholic Hierarchy give 17 September 965 as the start of the episcopate). He attended the Synod of Ingelheim (972) and the Diet of Speyer (984), joined Otto II's Italian campaign in 981/982, and left a versified catalogue of the bishops of Strasbourg plus marginal verse and prose notes. A Passio sancti Thrutberti is also attributed to him (Biblissima), though it is not among the works held here. Sources differ slightly on his death date: 11 October 991 per the Alsatian history federation and Wikidata, 12 July or 10 October 991 per the Infothek der Scholastik.
b.s: The works held here are chiefly his Leges municipales for the city of Strasbourg — rules asserting that sanctuary protects fugitives from violent seizure, that stolen goods may not be harbored there, that captives must be surrendered to judicial authority, that the bishop appoints all city magistrates, that offices are reserved to members of the bishop's church, that clergy may not bear the sword, that jurisdiction derives from emperor or bishop alone, and that subordinate judges are limited to debt cases — showing a tenth-century bishop legislating civic order under episcopal authority.

w: Fragments from the book On Grammar

b.bio: Ermanric of Reichenau is represented in the library by grammatical fragments preserved in PL 116. No biographical details about him can be confirmed from the retrieved sources: the source on 'Ermanrich of Passau' concerns a ninth-century bishop of Passau, a different person of the same name, and the sources on 'Hermann/Hermannus of Reichenau' concern an eleventh-century monk of that abbey, also a different person.
b.s: The library holds only fragments of his book On Grammar (PL 116), which in these pages treats faith, grace, charity as mother of the virtues, true royal power as virtue rather than territory, and the merit of saints' invocation, arguing against Gozpert and citing Charles, Louis, and Walahfrid.

w: On the Deeds of Louis the Pious

b.bio: Ermoldus Nigellus ('Ermold the Black') was a poet at the court of Pippin of Aquitaine, son of Emperor Louis I. He accompanied Pippin on the campaign into Brittany in 824 and was later banished from court for an undisclosed offence against Pippin and Louis; his poems were written in exile to regain favour and return to Aquitaine. The 1911 Britannica calls him a monk of Aquitaine, identifies him with a Hermoldus who was Pippin's chancellor in 838, and dates his recall to about 830, but Wikipedia notes that monastic status cannot be proven from his own works and that recent scholarship leans away from it. His chief work, In honorem Hludovici imperatoris, covers Louis's life from 781 to 826.
b.s: The library holds his verse panegyric on Louis the Pious, which argues that kingship is granted by Christ rather than human favor, that a ruler must love Christ, cultivate the church, venerate saints' relics, and rule justly, and that baptized rulers deserve admonition before war — an early statement of Carolingian political theology.

b.bio: Ervisius (also printed Ernisius) was an Englishman who served as abbot of Saint-Victor in Paris during the twelfth century. The sources that mention him do so chiefly through his successor: Richard of Saint Victor served as subprior (from 1159) and then prior under him and found his administration burdensome; the DNB says he ruled the house ill and was forced to resign in 1172, when Guarin was elected in his place. No dates of birth or death are given for him. The letters held here are addressed to or concern figures of his circle — King Louis, Pope Alexander III, bishops and abbots including Laurence of Westminster and Richard of Bristol — and deal with baptism, restitution owed by a knight named Ursinus, a vacant church's return to its founding monastery, and the claim that outward order sustains inward religious virtue.
b.s: Apart from the complaints of Richard of Saint Victor about his abbacy, the four pages of letters held here appear to be among the few surviving traces of him.

b.bio: The library prints this name over two short legal texts in PL 80: a Decree and Donations setting fines and compensations owed to the king — twofold payment for injury at his assembly or feast, ninefold for theft from him, fifty shillings for homicide in his villa or breach of his protection, threefold restitution between freemen plus royal forfeiture. These are early Anglo-Saxon royal ordinances, not the work of the eighth-century Archbishop Ethelbert of York described in the encyclopedias supplied, who taught Alcuin at the York school and died 8 November 781/782; that man is a different bearer of the name and is not the author of what is held here.
b.s: The texts preserved under this name are among the earliest written Anglo-Saxon legislation, fixing the king's share in compensation payments and marking the point where customary wergild practice entered written form.

b.bio: Æthelwulf (Latinised sometimes as Lupus Clarus) was a ninth-century Anglo-Saxon monk, known as the author of the Latin poem Carmen de abbatibus, an 819-hexameter poem recounting the history of his own house. Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 96 gathers under his name, alongside that poem, a body of canonical and liturgical material of Irish provenance: canons on church order, ordination, episcopal conduct, eucharistic sacrifice, and duties to the dead, together with notes on synods. The canon material cites Patrick, Gildas, and the Irish synods, and argues against the Britons, Eustathius, the Novatians, and heretical princes.
b.s: The works held here are chiefly Irish ecclesiastical canons on church governance, sacraments, and penitential practice preserved under Æthelwulf's name in PL 96, plus his historical poem on his abbey's abbots.

b.bio:
Euclid of Megara (c. 435–c. 365 BC) — Euclid of Megara was a Greek Socratic philosopher, a pupil of Socrates and present at his death in 399 BC. He founded the Megarian school, whose followers were later called Eristics and Dialecticians. He held the supreme good to be one, eternal, and unchangeable, denying that anything contrary to the good exists. The work shelved under his name here, a Geometry printed in PL 63, is not his: medieval editors and translators often confused him with Euclid of Alexandria, the author of the Elements, and the text's definitions and proofs of triangle properties belong to that geometric tradition.

Boethius (c. 475–480 – 524–526) — Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, born in Rome into the patrician Anicii family, was orphaned young and raised by Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, whose daughter Rusticiana he married. He served the Ostrogothic king Theoderic as senator, consul, and magister officiorum before his execution at Pavia around 524–526; the diocese of Pavia honors him as a martyr on 23 October (cult sanctioned 1883). Sources differ slightly on his dates: Wikipedia gives c. 480–524, the Stanford Encyclopedia c. 475–7 to 526?, Routledge c. 480–525/6. His project of translating Greek logic into Latin made him a principal conduit between ancient philosophy and the medieval Latin West.
b.s: He matters as founder of the Megarian dialectical school; the Geometry held here is a misattribution arising from the long-standing confusion between him and the geometer Euclid of Alexandria.

b.bio: Eugenius was unanimously elected Bishop of Carthage in 480 to succeed Deogratias, his election having been deferred by the Arian Vandal kings until permitted by Huneric at the instance of Zeno and Placidia. He defended the divinity of the Word against Arian theologians in a royal conference held between 481 and February 484, admitted Vandals into the Catholic Church contrary to royal edict, and after the conference was exiled by Huneric to the desert of Tripoli under the custody of one Antonius. On setting out he wrote a letter of consolation and exhortation to the faithful of Carthage. He died on 13 July 505 at Vienne and is honored as a saint.
b.s: The work held here is a Profession of Faith from a bishop whose confession cost him exile under Vandal Arian persecution; he stands as a witness to Nicene orthodoxy in late-fifth-century Africa.

b.bio: The library prints his name as Eugene III of Toledo; most modern sources number him Eugenius II or 'the Younger,' the third being reserved for a legendary first bishop of Toledo. Son of a Goth named Evantius, he was a cleric at Toledo and archdeacon to Braulio of Zaragoza before King Chindaswinth compelled him to accept the see of Toledo on the death of his predecessor in 647. He governed until his death on 13 November 657, attended the synods of Toledo of 653 and 656, reformed the chant of the Divine Office, and wrote prose and verse, including a recension of Dracontius's Hexaemeron poem.
b.s: The works held here — an epitaph, letters, and a preface from PL 87 — show a seventh-century Spanish prelate writing on the church, sacraments, prayer, and discipline, opposing simoniacs, deacons who usurped chrismation, and presbyters making their own chrism.

b.bio: Eumenius was a rhetorician of Augustodunum (Autun) in Gaul, of Greek descent through an Athenian grandfather who taught rhetoric there. He served as magister memoriae, private secretary, at the court of Constantius Chlorus, whom he accompanied on campaigns, and in 296/297 was appointed to manage the restored schools of Autun, surrendering part of his salary for their upkeep. The 1911 Britannica dates him c. 260–311; other references give only his floruit around 290–300, since neither birth nor death year is recorded. He was a pagan, not even nominally Christian.
b.s: The library holds two speeches addressed to Constantine — the Panegyric and the Gratiarum Actio (Act of Thanksgiving) — which praise Constantine's rule as resting on heredity and merit, pair his victories with clemency, and argue against Maxentius and other princes; they are primary evidence for how Constantine's reign was publicly framed before his conversion became explicit policy.

b.bio: Eusebius Bruno was trained under Berengar of Tours and made Bishop of Angers in December 1047. He attended the synod of Reims in 1049 under Leo IX, protesting his innocence regarding simony. After the councils of Rome and Vercelli condemned Berengar in 1050, he wrote protesting the injustice done to his teacher; he and Berengar both avoided a royal synod at Paris in 1051 for fear of condemnation. Contemporary writers Deoduinus of Liège and Durandus of Troarn classed him among Berengar's followers.
b.s: The letter held here is a eucharistic polemic asserting that bread becomes Christ's true body at consecration by divine omnipotence alone, written against Lanfranc and Geoffrey Martin and citing Ambrose, Hildebrand, and the apostolic see.

b.bio: Eusebius Pamphili, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine from about 313/314, was a historian, exegete, and polemicist trained under the presbyter Pamphilus, whose name he took after Pamphilus's martyrdom in 310. He lived through the Great Persecution and Constantine's reign, subscribed to the Creed of the Council of Nicaea (325) and explained his subscription in a letter to his diocese, and produced the Ecclesiastical History, the Chronicle, apologetic works such as the Preparation for and Demonstration of the Gospel, and the Life of Constantine. The library shelves him among Latin Fathers, but he wrote in Greek; readers should note this mislabeling.
b.s: The works held here show his two sides: the Life of Constantine presents a providential political theology in which victory comes through prayer to God rather than divination, God grants empire to pious rulers such as Constantine, and destroys persecuting tyrants like Licinius and Maxentius; while the Gospel Canons are his canon tables, a scholarly apparatus for reading the four Gospels together that shaped biblical study for centuries.

w: Fragment from a sermon against St. Cyril

b.bio:
Eutherius of Tyana (fl. 431–433) — Eutherius of Tyana was metropolitan bishop of Tyana in Cappadocia and a member of the eastern delegation led by John of Antioch at the Council of Ephesus (431). Before the council he corresponded with John of Antioch about the alleged Apollinarianism of Cyril of Alexandria and his adherents. On July 18, 431 he was deposed and excommunicated alongside John and his party, with the sentence confirmed at Constantinople before year's end. He wrote a protest against Cyril's condemnation of Nestorius, which brought his own deposition and exile to Scythopolis in Palestine. After John's reconciliation with Cyril in the Act of Union of 433, Eutherius escaped Scythopolis and took refuge with Irenaeus, bishop of Tyre.

Marius Mercator (c. 390–after 451) — Marius Mercator, probably born in Northern Africa about 390, died shortly after 451. In 417 or 418 he was in Rome, where he wrote two anti-Pelagian treatises and submitted them to Augustine of Hippo, who answered him in Epistula 193. From 429 to about 448 he lived in Constantinople. His writings are polemics against Pelagianism and Nestorianism and compilations of excerpts from Greek writers — Cyril of Alexandria, Nestorius, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret — which preserved the documents of the Nestorian controversy in Latin.
b.s: The fragment held here is NOT Eutherius's own protest: per the library record it is an anti-Nestorian polemic that argues against Eutherius himself and the followers of Nestorius, asserting that Christ suffered passibly like those he represents, that either Christ truly suffered or no man suffered, that an impassible passion destroys Christ's patience and love, and that refuting deniers of felt suffering risks a false 'Nestorian' label. It cites Marius Mercator and John, bishop of Tomis in Scythia.

b.bio: Eutrandus Ticinensis Diaconus, a deacon of Pavia, is known through a single work, the Chronicon printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 80. In its dedicatory letter he writes as a former subdeacon at Toledo under Bishop Bonito who carried historical books from Spain to Italy, and as an exile then residing in the monastery of Fulda. He addresses the work to Regimundus, bishop of Elvira, whom he describes as enduring hardship among the Saracens. The Documenta Catholica Omnia catalogue dates him 645–645, but the chronicle itself runs to the Spanish era 960 (AD 922), so the catalogue date cannot be right.
b.s: His sole held work is a short chronicle continuing Maximus of Saragossa's continuation of Dexter's chronicle down to his own time, touching on the Church and Scripture and citing Isidore, Ildefonsus, Elipandus, Charlemagne, and Trithemius.

b.bio: The Eutropius of this record is not Flavius Eutropius, the fourth-century Roman official and pagan historian of the Breviarium (fl. 363–387), but a distinct monastic author whose ascetical writings were printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 80). The surviving records describe only the historian, so nothing can be asserted about this Eutropius' dates, place, or office. The two short treatises held under his name deal with the capital vices: they argue that later vices arise from preceding ones and must be fought in order, that vainglory and pride attack after spiritual victories, that each capital vice divides into daughter sins, and that victory over vice comes by grace rather than self-reliance.
b.s: His works here are brief Latin ascetical texts on the eight vices and monastic strictness, useful for tracing how capital-vice doctrine passed into the Latin West.

w: On the Rights and Privileges of the Roman Emperors

b.bio: The library prints this author as 'Eutropius the Lombard,' but no source under that name supplies dates or a career. The works held here do not match Flavius Eutropius, the fourth-century historian of Rome (fl. 363–387), whose Breviarium Historiae Romanae is a different work entirely. The 'Letter to Pope Peter' corresponds to the correspondence of Eutropius of Valencia, a Spanish monk and later bishop (d. c. 610), who wrote preserved letters to Peter, Bishop of Iturbica — though no source confirms that the author printed here as 'Eutropius the Lombard' is that man. The historical tract on imperial rights, treating Charlemagne, Pope Zacharias, and Pope Leo, has no support in either source and stands on the library record alone.
b.s: The works held here are a polemical history asserting that imperial rights over papal ordination passed from the Romans to the Franks after Charlemagne's intervention in Italy, plus a letter to Bishop Peter.

w: On the Ten Names of God, Another Copy

b.bio: Evagrius of Antioch, son of Pompeianus, was a presbyter of the Eustathian party in Antioch. He accompanied Eusebius of Vercelli to Italy around 363–364, aided Pope Damasus against Ursicinus, and opposed the Arian bishop Auxentius at Milan. Returning east with Jerome, he was consecrated bishop by the dying Paulinus in 388 or 389, a rival to Flavian during the Meletian schism; Socrates and Sozomen say he survived his elevation only briefly, and he must have lived until at least 392. He is best known for his Latin translation of Athanasius's Vita Antonii, which supplanted an earlier version and circulated widely in the Middle Ages.
b.s: His Latin Vita Antonii carried Athanasius's portrait of Antony, and with it the model of monastic life, to the medieval West; the library holds that translation plus a short work on the ten names of God.

b.bio: Evantius of Troclara (Latin: Evantius Troclariensis) was a Hispanic writer and archdeacon who died in 737. The library holds one work under his name, a short epistle printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 88). He should not be confused with Evantius of Vienne, the late sixth-century bishop of Vienne who attended the councils of Mâcon, Lyon, and Valence; that figure belongs to a different century and left no such epistle. The epistle is a polemical and exegetical letter, not the work of the Gallic bishop.
b.s: His epistle defends Christian liberty in matters of food against heretics and schismatics, arguing that all foods are clean to the pure, that defilement comes from the heart not from foods, that the apostolic decree of Acts 15 was a temporary accommodation, and that the blood prohibition is to be read spiritually as forbidding works of iniquity.

b.bio: The library's record shows a single-page Latin text on the virtues of stones, printed under the name Evax in PL 171. The name Evax belongs to a figure of medieval lapidary literature: a supposed king or sage to whom treatises on stones were attributed, writing in the voice of one addressing Tiberius and Lucinius Fronto — names that appear as citations in this very page. the surviving records here describe Avitus of Vienne, Evagrius, and other writers entirely unrelated to a lapidary; they are homonyms or irrelevant hits and are disregarded. No source in hand gives dates, birthplace, or office for Evax, so none is asserted.
b.s: The work held here is a lapidary claiming esoteric knowledge of stones must be kept secret, asserting that stones possess individual virtues and hierarchies, and boasting that no book surpasses it — a specimen of the pseudo-Evax tradition that medieval readers took as an ancient authority on gems.

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Evodius of Uppsala,' but no source supports a Swedish connection; every source identifies him as Evodius, bishop of Uzalis in proconsular Africa, and the work held here — the De fide printed in PL 31 among Augustine's appendices — is his De fide contra Manichaeos. Born at Tagaste around the middle of the fourth century, he was Augustine's lifelong friend, became bishop of Uzalis in 396 or 397, took part in the controversies against the Donatists and Pelagians, and wrote to the monks of Adrumetum in 427. His precise death date is not known: Smith's Dictionary finds no trace of him after 427, the Biblical Cyclopedia says he died about 430, and the Lexikon für Theologie und Kirche gives 10 October 424.
b.s: His extant De fide contra Manichaeos, preserved with Augustine's works, is the principal surviving treatise by this correspondent and dialogue partner of Augustine.

b.bio:
Ezelo of Cluny (unknown) — Hézelon (also printed Etzelo or Ezelo) came from an aristocratic family of the Liège region; his uncle was Conrad I, Count of Luxembourg. A canon at Liège, he was called to Cluny, where he was a monk and oversaw construction of the great abbey church (Cluny III) begun in 1088. Peter the Venerable addresses him as magister, and Hildebert of Lavardin records that he wrote a life of Saint Hugh of Cluny. That Vita is otherwise lost; the work held here, treating Hugh's chastity from childhood, governance by virtue and example, imperial patronage binding rulers to Cluny, visions confirming his grace, prayers delivering captives from tyrants, and opposition to simoniacs, survives under his name in PL 159. Some older authorities identify 'Ezelo Cluniacensis' with Gilo of Toucy/Paris, cardinal-bishop of Tusculum, who also wrote a Vita of Hugh.

Gilo of Paris (d. 1139×1142) — Gilo of Paris, also called Gilo of Toucy or Gilo of Tusculum, was born in Toucy in the county of Auxerre and lived in Paris before becoming a monk at Cluny. A priest first, he was made cardinal-bishop of Tusculum between 1121 and 1123 and served as papal legate four times: to Poland and Hungary around 1124, to Carinthia in 1126, to the Crusader states in 1128 or 1129, and to Aquitaine from 1131 to 1137. He sided with Antipope Anacletus II in the schism of 1130 and was deposed by the Second Lateran Council in 1139.
b.s: He matters as the master builder of Cluny III and as hagiographer of Abbot Hugh of Cluny; the work here is held to be connected with that otherwise lost Vita.

w: Speech at the Council of Frankfurt

b.bio: Henry II, called Saint Henry, was the last emperor of the Saxon (Ottonian) dynasty. Born 6 May 973 in Bavaria, he succeeded his father as Duke of Bavaria in 995, became King of the Romans after Otto III's death in 1002, King of Italy in 1004, and was crowned emperor by Pope Benedict VIII in 1014. Educated at the cathedral school of Hildesheim, he died without an heir on 13 July 1024 and was canonized by Pope Eugenius III in 1146. The library holds his charters and diplomas from PL 140: grants to churches and monasteries asserting perpetual donation, exemption from secular jurisdiction, and royal protection against burdensome advocates.
b.s: His diplomas are primary evidence for Ottonian-Salian royal church policy — the theology of kings as donors and protectors of ecclesiastical property — rather than doctrinal treatises.

b.bio: Henry III, son of Conrad II, was German king from 1039 and Holy Roman emperor from his coronation by Clement II in 1046 until his death at Bodfeld in the Harz on 5 October 1056. A Salian, he held the duchies of Bavaria, Swabia, and Carinthia before succeeding his father, ended the papal schism of 1046, and was the last emperor able to dominate the papacy and a powerful advocate of the Cluniac reform movement. Sources give his birth date variously as 28 October 1017 (Britannica, Catholic Encyclopedia) or 28 October 1016 (Wikipedia). The library holds a three-page set of imperial constitutions from PL 151: legal enactments on clerical immunity from compulsory oaths, marriage with a brother's widow, poisoners, fealty, and benefices.
b.s: The constitutions here show an emperor legislating for religion and clergy—canons given force of imperial law—typifying the sacral exaltation of kingship that preceded the Investiture Contest.

b.bio: Henry IV, son of Henry III, became king of Germany in 1056 and emperor, ruling until his death in 1106. His reign was dominated by the Investiture Controversy with Pope Gregory VII over control of episcopal appointments, which brought his excommunication and his penance at Canossa in 1077, and later rebellion led by his own son. The works held here are not treatises but acts of government: royal diplomas granting churches privileges, immunities, and rights of abbatial election, and constitutions regulating monasteries.
b.s: His charters show how a king embroiled in the investiture conflict used grants to churches—free abbatial election, immunity, protection—as instruments of rule, making them primary evidence for royal-ecclesiastical relations before and during the Gregorian crisis.

b.bio: This name in the library stands for the anonymous imperial author of a single two-page letter addressed to Robert of Flanders, printed in PL 155. None of The surviving records identifies which emperor wrote it — they concern Demetrios Kydones, Maximus Planudes, Nicholas of Methone and Michael Psellus, i.e. different persons — so no reign dates or personal details are asserted here. The letter itself is an appeal for Latin military aid: it argues that Greek Christians oppressed by Turks and Pechenegs perish in body and soul, that Constantinople will fall without swift help, and that its relics and treasures must be defended.
b.s: The held work is an early Byzantine appeal to the Latin West for armed aid against the Turks and Pechenegs, treating the defense of Constantinople and its relics as a Christian duty.

w: Confirmation of the Election of Calixtus II
On the Miracles of Eugene III
Various readings and additions to the Chronicle of Bec

b.bio: Edmond Martène (22 December 1654 – 20 June 1739) was a French Benedictine historian and liturgist of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. Born at Saint-Jean-de-Losne near Dijon, he entered the abbey of Saint-Rémy at Reims in 1672 and was then sent to Saint-Germain to train under d'Achéry and Mabillon and assist with the Maurist edition of the Church Fathers. He spent his life in historical and liturgical scholarship, publishing a commentary on the Rule of St Benedict (1690), De antiquis monachorum ritibus (1690), De antiquis ecclesiae ritibus (1700), and, from 1708, collaborative work with Ursin Durand including the Veterum scriptorum collectio. The pieces held here are his editorial apparatus — admonitions, notices, preliminary observations, glosses and corrections — prefixed by him to texts he edited for the Patrologia Latina.
b.s: The works here are not treatises but Martène's editorial prefaces and notes on medieval texts he edited (Wibald of Stavelot's letters, the Chronicle of Bec, miracles of Eugene III, Abelard), showing how a leading Maurist prepared patristic and medieval sources for print.

b.bio: Paul Pétau is recorded in the theological library catalogue under the Latin Fathers tradition as the author of a held work titled Short Treatise.
b.s: He is catalogued as an author associated with Latin patristic or theological writings.

w: On the Lineage of the Counts of Braganza
Onomastic Index of Persons and Places
Prologue to the Life of Hermann

b.bio: Aemilian Ussermann, baptized Josef, was born 30 October 1737 at St. Ulrich in the Black Forest and died at St. Blasien on 27 October 1798 (the Oberdeutsche Personendatenbank gives 21 October). Educated at St. Peter in the Breisgau, he studied at Freiburg from 1754 (becoming Baccalaureus of Philosophy in 1755), entered St. Blasien in 1756, professed as a Benedictine there in 1757, and was ordained priest in 1761 (with dispensation). He taught moral theology and Hebrew literature at Salzburg, then returned to St. Blasien, where Abbot Martin Gerbert made him librarian and charged him with rebuilding the collection lost in the great fire of 1768. His lasting project was a Germania sacra, a historical account of all German dioceses; he personally produced the volumes on Würzburg and Bamberg.
b.s: The works held here are not his own theology but the scholarly apparatus of an editor: dissertations, prologue, preface, and indexes surrounding the medieval texts of PL 143, arguing against Wolfgang Lazius and Cesare Baronius/Canisius on points such as the lineage of the counts of Bregenz.

b.bio: The library holds one short work under this name, an Admonition printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 158. No surviving record identifies this author's dates, office, or life. He must not be confused with Giacomo Eugenio de Levis (1737–1810), an Italian priest of Turin who wrote on the cemetery of Santa Priscilla (1779) and collected monuments of Cisalpine history (1801); The surviving records describe only that later man, whose works do not match the item held.
b.s: His single held piece is a brief admonitory text preserved in PL 158; nothing further about him can be asserted from the materials at hand.

b.bio: Euthalius was a deacon of Alexandria who worked on the New Testament text around 459–460, dedicating his work to Athanasius, nephew of Cyril. The manuscripts style him deacon, not bishop; some later sources give him an otherwise obscure episcopal see called Sulca, but the record held here treats him as never having been a bishop. He divided Acts and the Epistles into sections for public reading, catalogued Old Testament quotations in the New Testament, and wrote a life of Paul.
b.s: His Euthalian Sections spread through the whole Greek Church and remain a dating tool for New Testament manuscripts; the work here presents his divisions and prolegomena to Acts and the Epistles.

w: Mark of Ephesus, Metropolitan of Ephesus

b.bio: Born Manuel Eugenikos in Constantinople, Mark became a monk at the monastery of Mangani and was made Metropolitan of Ephesus, representing the Patriarch of Alexandria at the Council of Ferrara–Florence (1438–1439). Initially open to union with Rome, he concluded during the council's commission work that Latin teaching conflicted with the dogmas of the Ecumenical Councils, and he alone among the Orthodox delegation refused to sign the decree of union, becoming the leader of the anti-unionist party. Sources disagree on his death: Britannica gives June 23, 1445; the Orthodox Church in America gives 1457 at age fifty-two.
b.s: The library holds his writings under PG 160 (one collected entry, 16 pages mined), which treat the Holy Spirit's procession, the sacraments, the Eucharist, baptism, the Church, Scripture, last things, and the Trinity, arguing against the Latins and the Florentine unionists — the theological case that made him the principal opponent of the Union of Florence.
